items.prose: A share ranks in the winner decile, then delists two months later with a −60% final return. Your source drops that final return.
items.question: What does the omission do to the measured spread?

options.text: Raises it: the long leg misses a loss
Lowers it: the short leg misses a gain
options.why: You put the share in the short leg. It ranked as a winner, so we hold it long.

options.text: Nothing: one share is too small to matter
options.why: You dismissed one share. A −60% month on a 1/50 weight moves the leg by over 1%.

feedback.correct: Correct. A dropped loss flatters the long leg.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which leg holds this share?

explain.text: The share sits in the long leg, so its missing −60% makes the long leg look better. The spread is then biased up. Had it been a loser, the bias would run the other way.

items.prose: A share has a NaN return in month 40. You rank with J = 6 and require six complete months.
items.question: In how many months is the share left out of the ranking?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which ranking windows contain month 40?

byKey.one: You left it out only in month 41. Every window up to month 46 still holds month 40.
byKey.seven: You counted month 40 itself. Its own ranking uses months 34 to 39, which are complete.

explain.text: The window for month t is t − 6 to t − 1. It contains month 40 when t runs from 41 to 46: 6 months. From month 47 the share ranks again.

items.prose: In one month 505 shares have full histories. Deciles are `rank * 10 // 505`.
items.question: How many shares are in the bottom decile?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the ranks r with r × 10 // 505 equal to 0.

byKey.fifty: You split 505 evenly. Ranks 0 to 50 all give decile 0: 51 shares.

explain.text: Ranks 0 to 50 give 0, so the bottom decile holds 51 shares. The counts alternate 51 and 50. Each loser then gets −1/51.

items.prose: Three formation windows for ranking in month $t$ with J = 6.
items.question: Which one has look-ahead?

options.why: You flagged the standard window. It ends the month before we trade.
You flagged the skip window. Ending earlier never uses future data.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Which window contains month t?

explain.text: Only $t - 5$ to $t$ contains month $t$, the month we then hold. Ranking on it earns that month's own returns: about 17% a month on our panel. The other two windows end before $t$.

items.prose: With K = 12, a share is a winner in 5 live cohorts and a loser in 2. Deciles hold 50 shares.
items.question: What is its composite weight?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the twelve cohort weights, signs and zeros included.

byKey.sum: You summed the cohorts. The composite averages them: divide by 12.
byKey.seven: You added the losers' weights as positive. Losers carry −1/50.

explain.text: Five cohorts give +0.02, two give −0.02 and five give 0. The sum is 0.06, and dividing by 12 gives 0.005. A share can sit in both legs of different cohorts.

items.prose: A 12/12 strategy with a one-month skip runs on 300 months.
items.question: How many composite returns does it give?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use T − J − skip − K + 1.

byKey.noskip: You left out the skip month. It delays the start by one.
byKey.blocks: You counted non-overlapping blocks. The composite gives a return every month.

explain.text: The first full composite is in month 12 + 1 + 12 − 1 = 24. Months 24 to 299 give 276 returns. Non-overlapping blocks would give only (300 − 13) // 12 = 23.

items.prose: On our panel the skip moves 3/3 from 0.51% to 0.86% and 12/12 from 0.66% to 0.57%.
items.question: Which explanation fits both moves?

options.text: The skip drops holding month 1, which reverses, and adds month K + 1, which is weak for long K
The skip spends a month in cash
options.why: You treated the skip as time out of the market. The book is invested every month.
You dismissed a pattern the generator plants: a one-month reversal and a slow long reversal.
The paper reports that for its data; on our panel 12/12 falls.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which holding month leaves and which joins.

explain.text: Month 1 carries the planted reversal, so dropping it helps 3/3 most. For 12/12 the added month 13 sits in the slow reversal. So the same swap helps one cell and hurts the other.

items.prose: Our 12/3 cell is 1.31% with se 0.41%. The paper reports about 1.31%.
items.question: What is the gap in standard errors, to two places?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the gap by the standard error.

byKey.pts: You gave the gap in points. Divide it by the standard error.

explain.text: The gap is 0.01 standard errors, far inside 2. Our panel was tuned to the paper, so a close match is expected. It tests our code, not momentum.

items.prose: A colleague's 6/6 came out at 0.70%. He then reports the version among 18 designs that gives 0.95%.
items.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: The match is the product of the search, so it is no evidence
It is fine because 6/6 is the paper's design
options.why: You accepted the label. He changed the skip and the windows until the number fitted.

options.text: It is fine if the gap is under 2 standard errors
options.why: You applied the matching rule. The rule assumes the design was fixed first.

options.text: He should search more designs to be sure
options.why: You asked for more search. That makes a match even less informative.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask when the design was chosen.

explain.text: With 18 tries, one landing near 0.95% is almost certain. A rule like 2 standard errors only means something for a design fixed in advance. This is the data snooping the testing course warns about.
